grand_strategy.reading:
Uzbekistan is the one state in the region whose strategy is a strategy of
position: doubly landlocked, the most populous in Central Asia and the youngest
of the big populations (a median age near 27), it has turned its geography
from a prison into a toll. Luttwak's logic runs the other way from the
great powers' - the weak do not win by force but by being the crossing that
several strong actors each need and none can take. Since 2016 Mirziyoyev
has traded the Karimov-era isolation for a portfolio of partners (Carnegie's
word for it): rail to China, rail to Pakistan through Afghanistan, Rosatom and
Gazprom for power, Gulf money for solar, Washington and Brussels for minerals
and legitimacy, Seoul and Tokyo for factories, Delhi for the Indian Ocean route
and a Treaty on Allied Relations with each Turkic neighbour that is not an
alliance in the military sense. The 2023 constitution is the domestic hinge:
the opening abroad is the means by which a reset presidency keeps its
stability. The paradoxes all take the same shape - each exit from one
dependence is an entry into another: Russian power for Russian gas, Chinese rail
for Chinese goods, the Taliban corridor for the Taliban's canal, remittances for
Russia's lever. The gold reserve is the one buffer that belongs to Tashkent
alone, and the central bank's decision to keep it at home tells how it
reads the risk. Watch two signals that are not rows: the 17% of the Chinese
railway built by August 2026 (the first real test of whether the toll works) and
the 29-30 Oct Ankara summit of the Turkic states after Mirziyoyev's trip to
Ashgabat for the CIS summit (7-9 Oct, outcomes unconfirmed).

stances.note: Both capitals call it a 'comprehensive strategic partnership and alliance' (Mirziyoyev-Putin, St Petersburg, 4 Jun 2026, trade up 20% since January), but the structure is partnership: no CSTO membership, only observer status in the EAEU (Dec 2020, still the line in Oct 2024), neutrality on Ukraine thanked by Putin (Jun 2024). The ties that bind are material - remittances (72.4% of inflows from Russia in Q1 2026), gas (6.48 bcm in 2025), Rosatom (first concrete 24 Mar 2026) and more than a quarter of gasoline - and the friction is real (June 2025 protest at the treatment of Uzbek migrants). Carnegie reads it as Russia failing to deliver in specific sectors, which is why Tashkent diversifies. Not 'ally': no mutual defence and the 'alliance' wording is rhetoric. Bond - affinity: Soviet legacy, language and 1.34 million Uzbeks working in Russia, without kinship.
